**1) Correlation of 2017 and 2018 New Haven Road Race Times**.

On homework 5 you created a dataset called `nhcombined` that had times for runners who ran in both the 2017 and 2018 New Haven Road Race AFTER removing unusual observations. I've put the final resulting dataset [HERE](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jreuning/sds230_data/refs/heads/main/nhcombined.csv).

```{r}
nhcombined <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jreuning/sds230_data/refs/heads/main/nhcombined.csv")
  
dim(nhcombined) #985, 5 - this is the same as the data in hw5
names(nhcombined)
head(nhcombined)
```


(1.2)  Find the code that defines the functions `myCor()` (class 11) and `permCor()` (class 12).   Paste the code for both functions in a chunk below.  Run each function on net times in 2018 and 2017 for runners in your `nhcombined` dataset to make a scatterplot of these times and to run a permutation test on the correlation between times (i.e. we're seeing if times from one year to the next are correlated within runners).  Be sure to include the resulting histogram and the p-value of the test.  Does it seem appropriate to calculate correlation (think about outliers)?

```{r}
# myCor() function
myCor <- function(x, y){
  #make the scatterplot
  plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "red")
  #add text in the margin reporting the sample correlation)
  mtext(paste("Sample Correlation =", round(cor(x, y), 3)), side = 3, cex = 1.2)
}
# permCor() function
#The option below prevents R from using scientific notation!
options(scipen = 999)

permCor <- function(x, y, n_samp = 10000, plotit = T){
   corResults <- rep(NA, n_samp)
   for (i in 1:n_samp){
      corResults[i] <- cor(x, sample(y))
   }
   
   pval <- mean(abs(corResults) >= abs(cor(x, y)))
   
   if (plotit == T){
      #Make histogram of permuted correlations
      hist(corResults, col = "yellow", main = "", xlab = "Correlations", breaks = 50,
           xlim = range(corResults,cor(x,y)))
      mtext("Permuted Sample Correlations", cex = 1.2, line = 1)
      mtext(paste0("Permuted P-value = ", round(pval, 4),", Calculated P-value = ", round(cor.test(x, y)$p.value, 4)), cex = 0.8, line = 0)
      abline(v = cor(x, y), col = "blue", lwd = 3)
      text(cor(x,y)-.02, 0, paste("Actual Correlation =", round(cor(x, y), 2)), srt = 90, adj = 0) # changed x of text to be in viewing panel
   }
   if (plotit == F){
      return(round(pval, 5))
   }  
}

# run on nettimes in 2018 and 2017 for runners in dataset
myCor(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018)
permCor(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018)

# scatterplot of times 
plot(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018,
     main = "Scatterplot of Nettimes for Runners in 2017 and 2018",
     ylab = "2018 Time",
     xlab = "2017 Time",
     col = "coral",
     pch = 4,
     lwd = 2
     )

# permutation test on correlation between times 
n_samp <- 10000

corResults <- rep(NA, n_samp)

for(i in 1:n_samp){
  corResults[i] <- cor(sample(nhcombined$Nettime_2017), sample(nhcombined$Nettime_2018))
}

# histogram of permutation and p value of test
truecor <- mean(abs(corResults) >= abs(cor(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018)))

hist(corResults, col = "yellow", main = "", xlab = "Permuted Correlations", breaks = 50, xlim = c(-.15, .8)) # manually added xlim to see abline

mtext("Permuted Sample Correlations", cex = 1.2, line = 1)
mtext(paste0("Permuted P-value = ", round(truecor, 4),", Calculated P-value = ", round(cor.test(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018)$p.value, 4)), cex = 0.8, line = 0)

abline(v = cor(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018), col = "blue", lwd = 3)
text(cor(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018)-.02, 300, paste("Actual Correlation =", round(cor(nhcombined$Nettime_2017, nhcombined$Nettime_2018), 2)), srt = 90) # manually changed where text appears 

```
*No it is not appropriate to calculate correlation on the raw values as there seems to be large outliers (3 specifically stick out) that are likely pulling the correlation.*

**2) Correlation and the Bootstrap**. 

**World Bank Data: CO2 Emissions per capita and Energy Use per capita**  

A `.CSV` file containing world bank data from 2016 can be downloaded [HERE](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jreuning/sds230_data/refs/heads/main/WB.2016.csv).

The variables we'll consider in this example are:

* `Country` : countryname
* `EnergyUse`: kilograms of oil equivalent usage per capita
* `CO2`: CO2 emissions per capita (metric tons)

In this problem, we will take a closer look at the correlation between Energy Use per capita and CO2 Emissions per capita.

(2.1)  Read the data into an object called `wb`. Then make a dataframe called `wb2` that has complete data but only contains the country name, EnergyUse and CO2.  Finally, create two new variables `logEnergy` and `logCO2` which are the natural log of each of these variables, respectively. You only need to retain these 5 columns in `wb2`.

```{r}
# read in data as wb
wb <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jreuning/sds230_data/refs/heads/main/WB.2016.csv")
dim(wb)
names(wb)

# make dataframe wb2 that is complete data of country, energy and co2
wb2 <- wb[, c("Country", "EnergyUse", "CO2")] # already dataframe
 
# omit rows that have NA aka only keeps complete data 
wb2 <- na.omit(wb2)
rownames(wb2) <- NULL # resets row index to be 1, 2, 3... after saving only complete data

# make sure no values are 0 that would require adding a base 
range(wb2$EnergyUse) # no 0s
range(wb2$CO2) # no 0s

# create new variable logenergy
wb2$logEnergy <- log(wb2$EnergyUse)

# create new variable logCO2
wb2$logCO2 <- log(wb2$CO2)

# check dim of wb2 to ensure only 5 columns remain
dim(wb2)
names(wb2)

# check there are no na
sum(is.na(wb2)) # 0!
```

Then make a scatterplot of CO2 (vertical axis) and EnergyUse (horizontal axis) on both the raw scale and the log scale.  Put appropriate labels on all plots and make them look interesting (i.e. use a non-default color at least). Add the correlation to two decimal places between variables as a subtitle. *Both variables on a raw scale are right skewed. In log scale, they are closer to normal distribution.*

There are some outliers on the raw scale that might make correlation not the best analysis. On the log scale, these outliers are not present. This is perhaps reflected in the value of the correlation because the correlation is stronger on the log scale compared to the raw scale. Both correlations are strongly positive.*

(2.4)  Calculate (and display) a parametric test of the significance of the correlation between logCO2 and logEnergy, and save the result in an object called `cor1test`.  Is the correlation statistically significantly different from zero?  What is a 96% confidence interval for the location of the true correlation?

```{r}
# parametric test of significance of correlations between logCO2 and logEnergy
cor1test <-  cor.test(wb2$logCO2, wb2$logEnergy)
cor1test

# 96% confidence interval of true correlation 
truecor <- cor.test(wb2$logCO2, wb2$logEnergy, conf.level = 0.96)
truecor
```


*Yes, with a p value of essentially 0, it is likely the true correlation is not equal to 0 evaluated at any alpha level.*
*A 96% confidence interval places that the location of the true correlation is between 0.89 and 0.94.*

(2.5)  Get 10000 bootstrap samples from `wb2` following the example given in Class 11.  For each sample, calculate the correlation of log(CO2) and log(Energy Use) in your sample - save results in an object called `corResults`. Calculate a 96% bootstrap confidence interval for the true correlation based on quantiles.  Save results in an objects called `ci_r` (for correlation).  Display the results for these intervals.

```{r}
# 10000 bootstrap samples 
corResults <- rep(NA, 10000)
data <- wb2 
N <- nrow(data) # calculate number of row

for(i in 1:10000){
  #get vector of rows in our fake sample
  s <- sample(1:N, N , replace = T) # taking sample of row numbers that will be chosen, sometimes more than once because done with replacement
  
  #Calculate unique rows in our sample
  sVals <- as.numeric(names(table(s))) # extracts unique row numbers selected 
  
  #Calculate how many times each row shows up
  sCounts <-  as.vector(table(s))
  
  #Get bootstrapped data - choose pairs of rows multiple times or not at all
  fakeData <-  data[s, ] # actually pulls rows of data 
    
  #calculates correlation 
  corResults[i] <- cor(fakeData[, 4], fakeData[,5])} # columns 4 and 5 are logEnergy and logCO2
    
# calculate 96% bootstrap ci for true correlation
ci_r <- quantile(corResults, c(0.02, 0.98))
round(ci_r, 2)
```

(2.6)  Make a histogram of the results in `corResults`.  Add vertical lines for both the theoretical confidence interval and the bootstrapped confidence interval.

```{r}
# histogram of corResults 
hist(corResults,
     main = "Correlation Results of 10000 Bootstrap Tests \n Between logCO2 and logEnergyUse",
     xlab = "Correlation Value",
     xlim = c(0.82, 1),
     col = "brown4")
abline(v = ci_r, col = "black", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
abline(v = truecor$conf.int, col = "grey", lwd = 3, lty = 3)
legend(0.82, 2500, c("Bootstrapped CI", "Theoretical CI"), lwd = 3, col = c("black","grey"), lty = c(2, 3))
```


(2.7)  Comment on any differences you observe between the bootstrapped CI and the theoretical CI.  

*The bootstrapped CI is wider than the theoretical CI on both the left and the right side. This could be due to the presence of some high and low values that when they are continually included or not included, can skew the data.*

**3) Class Survey Data** 

This questions involves cleaning and making bivariate plots of several variables from the class survey data.   I'm going to be less specific of what you need to do - I'll say that at this point you have all the tools you need to clean the data and make interesting plots.

Just run the code below to get the data and remind you of the variables that exist.

```{r}

survey <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jreuning/sds230_data/refs/heads/main/class.survey.csv", header = TRUE, as.is = T)
names(survey)
dim(survey) # 239 reponses on 17 questions 

#install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr) # load dplyr to use pipes
```

(3.1)   Clean the variable `ClassProb` so that all values are between zero and 1.  Assume that any value over 20 is in a percentage and should be changed to a probability.  Any value more than 1 but less than 20 should be changed to `NA`.  Make a nice looking histogram of the resulting data and comment on the shape of the distribution.

```{r}
# clean variable ClassProb with all values between 0-1
# examine ClassProb
survey$ClassProb
range(survey$ClassProb) # range from .5 to 100
str(survey$ClassProb) # already numeric

# check for NA or blanks before any manipulation
survey$ClassProb[survey$ClassProb == "" | is.na(survey$ClassProb)] # none are blank or empty

# change any value between 1 and 20 to be NA 
survey$ClassProb[survey$ClassProb > 1 & survey$ClassProb < 20] <- NA

# any value over 20 from percentage to probability 
survey$ClassProb[survey$ClassProb > 20] <- survey$ClassProb[survey$ClassProb > 20] / 100

# recheck survey$ClassProb
str(survey$ClassProb) # still numeric
range(survey$ClassProb) # 0.5 - 1 yay!
survey$ClassProb[survey$ClassProb == "" | is.na(survey$ClassProb)] # none are blank or empty

# histogram 
hist(survey$ClassProb,
     main = "Frequency of Response to ClassProb",
     xlab = "Probablity You Will Take the Class",
     col = "red4")
```


*The histogram is heavily left skewed. This is likely due to the fact probability is a strict range of 0-1. A lot of students felt likely to take the class, causing a lot of data to be bunched on the right side.*

(3.2)   Clean the variables `Social` and `Econ` so that they are integer and numeric on the scale 1 to 7.  Make a two-way table of the results.  Does it appear there is a relationship between these variables?

(3.3)   Make three scatterplots of `Social` and `Econ` - one on the raw scale, one with jittered results, one with radii proportional to the square root of the frequency. Follow the examples shown in Class 11. Each plot should include the correlation in the labels. 

```{r}
# scatterplot - raw scale
plot(survey$Social, survey$Econ,
     xlab = "Responses to Social",
     ylab = "Responses to Econ", 
     col = "lightsteelblue1",

     ylab = "Responses to Econ", 
     col = "lightsteelblue2",
     pch = 16)

#Turn table of occurances into a vector
freq <- as.vector(table(survey$Social, survey$Econ))

#gives every possible combination pair
x1 <- rep(c(1:7), 7)
y1 <- rep(c(1:7), each = 7)

plot(x1, y1, #plotting every combination possible
     xlab = "Responses to Social",
     ylab = "Responses to Econ", 
     col = "lightsteelblue3",

     pch = 16)
mtext("Scatterplot Between Social and Econ Survey Results", line = 1.5, font = 2)
mtext(paste("Correlation = ", round(cor.test(survey$Social, survey$Econ)$estimate, 2)), line = 0, font = 3)
text(x1[freq >0], y1[freq >0], freq[freq >0], cex = log(freq/max(freq)*3 + 1), col = "black") # add text on top of points, except 0

```


(3.4)  Write a quick function called `cleanIt()`  that cleans the variables `Exercise` and `Coursework` so that they are numeric.  Apply this function to these two variables (which by the way are in minutes) and make histograms of the results.  In a sentence, describe what you see.

```{r}
# explore Exercise and Coursework
survey$Exercise
survey$Coursework

# write function called cleanIt() cleaning variables Exercise and Coursework to be numeric
cleanIt <- function(data) {
  data <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", data)
  as.numeric(data)
}

survey$Coursework[is.na(as.numeric(survey$Coursework))]

# apply function to Exercise
survey$Exercise <- cleanIt(survey$Exercise)
#check structure
str(survey$Exercise)

# apply function to Coursework
survey$Coursework <- cleanIt(survey$Coursework)
#check structure
str(survey$Coursework)

# histogram of Exercise
hist(survey$Exercise,
     col = "maroon3",
     main = "Frequency of Exercise Answers in Survey",
     xlab = "Exercise Values",
     ylim = c(0, 100))

# histogram of Coursework
hist(survey$Coursework,
     col = "maroon4",
     main = "Frequency of Coursework Answers in Survey",
     xlab = "Coursework Values",
     ylim = c(0, 150))
```

*Both distributions are right-skewed, but they have different ranges. For both coursework and exercise, low value answers were the most popular but with coursework there are a lot of values under 500 with some high outliers out past 2000; with exercise, there is more values spread out amongst the whole range but the low values under 200 are still the most popular.*
